inline.s: If you set goals for the small self, such as liberating yourself, strengthening yourself, or making yourself feel important, then even if you attain these goals you will not feel fulfilled. Set goals, but understand that what matters is not only attaining them. Whatever arises in presence, it represents the fact that this moment is not a means to an end: the action itself already achieves itself in every moment. You no longer downgrade the present to being a mere means to reach a goal; such thinking belongs to the consciousness of the small self.
“With no self, there is no problem,” was how a great Buddhist master replied when people asked him to explain the deep meaning of the Buddha.

On the surface, it seems that the present moment is just one of very many moments. Each day of your life appears to be composed of tens of thousands of moments in which all kinds of things happen. Yet when you look more deeply, is there not only this one moment? Has life ever existed outside this moment? This moment, the now, is the only place you can never escape. It is the eternal element of your life. No matter what happens. No matter how your life changes. One thing is certain. It is always in the present. Since you cannot escape the present, why not open your arms to it and make friends with it.
When you become friends with this present moment, you will feel at home wherever you are. And when you do not feel at home in the present moment, then wherever you go you will carry unease with you.
The present moment always exists as it is. Can you let it be?

The division of life into past, present, and future is manufactured by the mind, and is essentially illusory. Both past and future are merely modes of thought, abstract concepts in the mind. The past can only be remembered in the present. What you remember is something that once happened at a present moment, and you are also remembering it in the present. The future, when it arrives, is also the present. Therefore the only thing that is real, the only thing that exists, is the present.

Paying attention to the present is not about denying the needs of your life. It means being aware of what is most important. Then you can handle secondary matters with ease. This is not saying: “I will never deal with affairs again, because only the present exists.” No. First discover that which is most important, and make the present your friend rather than your enemy. Face it, respect it. Once the present becomes the foundation and focus of your life, your life will unfold with ease.

Clearing away the dishes, devising a business strategy, planning a trip — what is truly more important: the process of doing, or the result you want to achieve by doing? This moment, or some future moment? Do you look upon this moment as an obstacle to be overcome? Do you feel that you want to reach some future moment, and that it is more important than the present? Almost everyone lives this way most of the time. Since the future never arrives, except as a present moment, this is a dysfunctional way of life. It produces a continual undercurrent of unease, tension, and dissatisfaction. It does not cherish life, and life is the present — there is nothing else besides the present.
Feel the aliveness of your inner body. It can anchor you in the present.

In essence, only when you take responsibility for this present moment are you taking responsibility for life. For the present is the only place where life abides. Taking responsibility for this moment means not resisting the “what is” of the present within, and not arguing with it. It means being in accord with life. The present is as it is because it cannot be otherwise. Now, scientists have verified what Buddhists have always known: nothing and no event exists independently. Beneath the surface phenomena, all things are interrelated; they are all parts of the unity of the universe, and in this present moment the universe brings forth all things. When you say “yes” to what is, you align with the power and the frequency of the intelligence of life itself. Only then can you become a conduit of positive energy that affects this world.
A simple yet highly transformative spiritual practice is this: accept whatever arises in the present — both inner and outer.

When you move your attention into the present, you feel an alertness. It is as if you were waking from a dream, the dream of thinking, the dream of past and future. So clear, so simple. There is no room to create problems. Only this moment as it is.

As you enter the present moment, you realize that life is sacred. When you are present, you discover that everything you perceive is sacred. The more you live in the present, the more you feel the simple and vast joy of “being,” and the sacredness inherent in all things.

Most people confuse the present with what happens in the present, but it is not that. The present is deeper than what happens in it. It is the space that holds them. So do not mix the content of this moment with the present. The present is deeper than any content that occurs within it.

When you enter the present, you step out of the content of the mind. That endless stream of thinking slows down. Thoughts no longer absorb all your attention, no longer drag you away entirely. A gap opens up between thoughts, and space and stillness. You begin to realize that compared with your thoughts, the real you is far vaster and deeper. Thoughts, emotions, perceptions, and everything you experience make up the content of your life. You derive your sense of self from “my life,” and “my life” is satisfying, or so you think. You constantly overlook the most obvious fact: your innermost sense of who you are has nothing to do with what happens in your life, nothing to do with content. That sense of who I am has to do with the present. It is always the same. Whether in childhood or old age, health or illness, success or failure, that I am — the space of the present — at its deepest core always remains unchanged. We often confuse it with content, and as a result you can only faintly, indirectly experience the I am, or the present, through the content of your life. In other words: your sense of “being” is veiled by your surroundings, the stream of your mind, and many other things in this world. The present is veiled by time. So you forget your roots in “being,” your sacred reality, and you lose yourself in this world. When people forget who they are, doubt, anger, depression, violence, and conflict arise. Yet how easy it is to recall the truth, to return home: I am not my thoughts, emotions, perceptions, and experiences. I am not the content of my life. I am life. I am the space where all things happen. I am consciousness. I am the present. I am.

At the deepest level, the present and the real you are inseparable. Many things in your life are urgent, but there is only one thing that is absolutely important. Whether you are successful, or in the eyes of the world a failure, this matters. Whether your body is well or unwell, whether you are learned or unlearned, it matters. Whether you are rich or poor, it matters. It will without doubt bring change to your life. Yes, relatively speaking, all these matters are important. But they are not absolutely important. There is something far more important than any of these, and that is to discover that your essence transcends this transient body, that the real you transcends this transient self-sense that has been labeled as a person. You cannot attain peace by changing the circumstances of your life; you can feel peace only when you realize at the deepest level who you truly are.
If in your next life you still do not know who you are, then even rebirth and reincarnation will not help you.

All the suffering on this planet stems from a sense of “I” or “we” that has been pasted on with labels. It conceals your true essence. When you ultimately remain entirely ignorant of your inner essence, you cannot help but create suffering. It is that simple. When you do not know who you are, you create a mind-made self as a substitute for your beautiful, sacred self, and you cling to this self that is full of fear and greed. You constantly protect and reinforce it, and this erroneous self becomes your primary driving force.

Many everyday expressions, and sometimes even the structure of language itself, reveal the fact that people do not know who they are. You say, “he lost his life,” or “my life,” as if life were something you could possess or lose. The truth is you do not have a life; you are life, this one life, this one consciousness that pervades the whole universe, that experiences itself through transient visible forms — like a stone, a blade of grass, an animal, a person, a star, or an entire galaxy. Can you feel in the depths of your being that you already know it? Can you feel that you already are it?

For most things in life you need time: to learn a new skill, build a house, become an expert, brew a cup of tea. Yet for the most essential thing in life you do not need time. This truly vital matter — self-realization — means realizing that the real you transcends the superficial small self, that it transcends your name, your body, your history, your story. You cannot find yourself in the past or the future. You can only find yourself in the present. Spiritual seekers always seek self-realization or enlightenment in the future. To be a seeker means you need the future. If this is what you think, then it becomes true for you. You will always need time to seek, until you discover that to become the real you requires no time.

When you look at a tree, you are aware of the tree. When you have a thought or a feeling, you are aware of that thought or feeling. When you have a pleasant or painful experience, you are aware of that experience. These all seem to be true and obvious statements. However, if you observe them very carefully, you will discover that within this very structure a basic illusion is subtly contained, and once you use language this illusion is unavoidable. Thought and language create an obvious duality, and a separate person, that do not really exist. The truth of the matter is that you are not the one who is aware of the tree, thought, feeling, or experience. You are that awareness or consciousness in which and through which these things appear. As you live your busy life, can you be aware of yourself as that awareness, within which your whole life content unfolds?

You say: “I want to know myself.” You are the subject, the I. You are the one who knows. You are consciousness itself, through which all things are known, and this consciousness cannot know itself. It is itself. There is nothing beyond it that is known. And all knowing comes from it. The subject I cannot turn itself into an object of knowledge or of consciousness. So you cannot be your own object. This is exactly where the illusion of the small self’s identity arises: in the mind you turn yourself into an object. “This is I,” you say, and then you begin to develop a relationship with yourself, and tell others and yourself a story about you.

By realizing that you are that pure consciousness, and that everything that appears to exist happens within it, you begin to be liberated from your dependence on phenomena, and you no longer seek a self in situations, status, or external conditions. In other words, what has happened or has not happened no longer seems so important. Things are no longer so heavy, so serious. A sense of play comes into your life. You see this world as a cosmic dance, a dance of forms. It is no more and no less than that.

When you know who you truly are, you feel a constant, vibrant stillness. You may call it joy, because joy is precisely this feeling — a living, vibrant stillness. It is the joy of knowing that you are the essence of life, before life takes on the burden of form. It is the joy of being, the joy of being the real you.

Just as water can be solid, liquid, or vapor, consciousness too can appear in different forms. It can be firm as an object, flowing as mind and thought, or formless as pure consciousness. Pure consciousness is precisely the state of life before its manifestation. This life looks upon this world of form through your eyes, because consciousness is you. When you realize you are consciousness, you can recognize yourself in all things. Your perception is so clear. You are no longer the person with a heavy past, which all along had been a screen of concepts that you used to interpret every experience. When you perceive without the interpretation of the mind, you can directly perceive the thing as it truly is. The most fitting words we can find are that, in an alert and still field, perception arises. Through you, formless consciousness becomes aware of itself. Most people’s lives are driven by desire and fear. Desire is wanting to add something to yourself, so as to feel more complete. And all fear is the dread of losing something, lest you be diminished or made smaller. Both kinds of behavior conceal a fact: being cannot be given or taken away. Perfect being is in you, in this present moment.

Whenever you can, look within and see whether you are unconsciously creating conflict between the inner and outer, between the outer environment of that moment — the place you are, the people you are with, what you are doing — and your thoughts and feelings. Can you feel how much you suffer when you resist what is? Once you recognize this, you also realize that you have the freedom to give up this useless struggle and stop the inner state of war.

How many times a day, if you were to put the inner reality of that moment into words, would you have to say, “I do not want to be here”? When you do not want to be here and now — in a traffic jam, at the workplace, in a waiting lounge, with that particular person — what do you feel? Of course, you should indeed leave some places — and sometimes that may be your best choice. But in many cases, leaving is not the way. In these situations, that thought “I do not want to be here” is not only useless but abnormal. It makes both you and those around you unhappy. There is an old saying: where the body is, there the mind is. In other words: you are right here. Always. Is it really so hard to accept this?

Do you really need to label every feeling and experience in your mind? When you are almost constantly in conflict with your surroundings and with people, do you really need to always have a like-or-dislike relationship with life? Or is this just a deep-rooted habit of the mind, a habit that can be broken? Nothing needs to be done; just allow this moment to be as it is.
The habitual reactive “no” reinforces the small self, while “yes” weakens it — your identity of form. This small self cannot survive in surrender.

“I have too much to do.” Yes, but what is the quality of your actions? Driving to work, meeting with clients, working at the computer, running errands, handling the countless trivial matters that make up your life — how engaged are you as you do them? Are you doing them in surrender, or reluctantly? This is where the success of your life is determined, and not by how much effort you expend. Effort implies pressure and tension, needing to reach some point in the future, or to attain some result. Can you detect even the slightest resistance to what you are doing? This is a denial of life, and as a result a truly successful outcome is impossible. If you can be aware of this internally, can you let go of the resistance and throw yourself completely into what you are doing?

“Do one thing at a time.” A Chan master once defined the essence of Chan in this way. Doing one thing at a time means putting your whole being into what you do, with complete attention. This is the action of surrender — action imbued with power.

Your acceptance of what is brings you into a deeper level within; at the same time, your sense of self no longer depends on the mind’s judgments of “good” and “bad.” When you say “yes” to the “what is” of life, when you accept the present moment as it is, you can feel within a great sense of space, and a deep peace. On the surface, you may still feel happy when the weather is fine, and less happy when it rains; you may feel happy when you gain a million dollars, and unhappy when you lose all your property. But these joys and unhappinesses will no longer reach into your depths. They are all only small waves on the surface of your being. Whatever the outer circumstances, your inner peace, which is like a background, can remain undisturbed. This “yes” to what is opens up a deeper dimension within you, one that depends neither on outer circumstances nor on that inner circumstance full of ever-fluctuating thoughts and emotions.

All experience is transient and fleeting, and this world cannot give you anything eternal and unchanging. When you realize this, surrender becomes much easier. Then you continue to relate to people, take part in experiences and activities, but without the greed and fear of the small self. This is to say: you no longer demand that a situation, a person, a place, or a thing should satisfy you or please you. The nature of life as constantly flowing and imperfect is accepted as it is. And the miracle is that when you stop imposing unrealistic demands upon the facts, every situation, every person, every place, or every thing begins to become satisfying, and more harmonious, more peaceful.

When you fully accept the present moment, when you no longer argue with what is, compulsive thinking gradually weakens and is gradually replaced by an alert stillness. You are completely awake, yet the mind no longer labels the present in any way. This inner state of non-resistance carries you into infinite consciousness, which is far greater than the human mind. Then this vast intelligence can express itself through you, and support you both within and without. This is why, by letting go of inner resistance, you will always find that your surroundings become better.
Am I saying: “Enjoy the present moment. Be happy”?
No. Allow the “what is” of the present to exist. That is enough.

Surrender means surrendering to the present moment, not to a story you have fabricated in order to interpret this moment, and which you then try to convince yourself to believe. For example, you may have a disability and can no longer walk. That is the situation. Perhaps your mind is fabricating a story: “My life has come to this. I am ending my days in a wheelchair. Life has been so cruel and unjust to me. I do not deserve this.”
Can you accept the reality of this present moment without mixing it with the story the mind is fabricating around it?
Only when you stop asking, “Why does this happen to me?” does surrender really come.

Even in the situations that seem most unacceptable and most painful, there is hidden a deeper good; in every disaster there is contained a seed of grace. Throughout history, there have been men and women who, when facing great loss, illness, imprisonment, or sudden death, accepted what seemed unacceptable, and so discovered “the peace that surpasses all understanding.” Accepting the unacceptable is the greatest source of grace in this world.

Sometimes all answers and explanations do not work. Life becomes incomprehensible. Or someone in pain comes to you for help, and you do not know what to do or say. When you fully accept that you do not know, you give up using the limited thinking mind to struggle for answers, and it is precisely at this moment that a greater intelligence can work through you. Even thinking itself can benefit from this, because this great intelligence can flow into the mind and inspire it. Sometimes surrender means abandoning the effort to always understand, and becoming comfortable with not knowing.

Do you know someone whose primary function in life seems to be to make themselves and others suffer, spreading unhappiness everywhere? Forgive them, because they too are part of the process of human awakening. The role they play represents an intensification of the nightmare of small-self consciousness, an intensification of the state of non-surrender. None of this has anything to do with the personal. It is not their true nature.

Surrender may be described as an inner transformation, from resistance to acceptance, from “no” to “yes.” When you surrender, your sense of self shifts, from identifying with a reaction or a judgment of the mind, to being the space around this reaction or judgment. This is a shift from identifying with outer form — thought or emotion — to realizing yourself as a formless — vast awareness — existence.
Whatever you fully accept will bring you into stillness, including accepting your non-acceptance, accepting that you are resisting.
Let life be as it is. Let it go with the flow.

We do not only rely on nature for what we need to survive. We also need nature to lead us back onto the road home, out of the prison of our own minds. We are lost in action, thinking, remembering, expecting — lost in a labyrinth of complex things, lost in a world full of problems. What the rocks, the grass, the trees, and the animals still know, we have forgotten. We have forgotten how to be — how to be quiet, how to simply be ourselves, how to dwell in the place where life resides: here and now.

Whenever you notice anything natural, anything that has come into existence without human interference, you step out of the prison of conceptual thinking, and to a certain degree you enter a state of connection with being, the state in which all natural things still abide. To notice a stone, a tree, or an animal does not mean to think about it, but simply to perceive it, letting your consciousness surround it. Then something of its nature is transmitted to you through it. You can feel how still it is, and by doing so the same stillness also rises within you. You feel how deeply it abides in being — completely one with everything happening in the present, one with the place where the present is. By realizing this, you too come to the resting place of the depths within.

When you walk or rest in nature, honor this field with your whole being. Be still. Look. Listen. Every animal and every tree is so at ease. Unlike humans, they have not split themselves in two. They do not live by a self-image in the mind, so they do not need to constantly try to protect or reinforce these images. The elk is itself. The daffodil is itself. All things in nature are not only one with themselves but also one with the whole. They have not separated themselves from the web of the whole, have not declared a separated existence: “I” and a universe other than me. Contemplation of nature can free you from that “I” — that great troublemaker.

Notice the many subtle sounds of nature — the rustling of leaves in the wind, the patter of raindrops falling, the buzzing of insects, the first song of birds at dawn. Give yourself to listening attentively. Beneath these sounds there is something greater: a sacredness that cannot be understood through thinking.

You did not create your body, and you cannot control its functions. A greater intelligence than the human mind is at work. It is this same intelligence that sustains all of nature. Through being aware of your inner energy field — feeling this vitality, this living presence within the body — you no longer have any distance from this intelligence.

A dog’s playfulness and joy, its unconditional love and state of being always ready to celebrate life, often forms a vivid contrast with the inner state of this dog’s owner — depressed, anxious, worried, lost in thinking, always unable to live in the only time and place that truly exists: here and now. One cannot help wondering: how can this dog, living day after day with such a person, still remain so sound, so joyful?

When you perceive nature only through the mind, only through thinking, you cannot feel its vitality, its being. You see only form, and know nothing of the life within the form — that sacred secret. Thought degrades nature into a commodity that can be used in the process of pursuing profit, acquiring knowledge, or pursuing other utilitarian ends. Ancient forests become lumber, a small bird becomes a research project, a mountain becomes something to be mined or conquered. When you perceive nature, make it a space without thought, without mind. When you approach nature in this way, it will respond to you and take part in human evolution and the awakening of planetary consciousness.
Carefully observe how present a flower is, how surrendered to life.

That plant you keep at home — have you ever truly looked at it? Have you ever let this being, at once familiar and mysterious, this thing we call a plant, teach you about its secret? Have you ever noticed how serene it is? Have you ever noticed how it is surrounded by a still field? In the moment you become aware of the stillness and serenity that a plant radiates, it becomes your teacher.

Observe an animal, a flower, a tree, and see how it abides in being. It is itself. It has supreme dignity, purity, and sacredness. Yet to see this you must go beyond the mind’s habit of naming and labeling. In the moment you see through the label of the mind, you feel the ineffable dimension of nature, one that cannot be comprehended by thought nor perceived through the senses. This is a harmony, a sacredness, that not only pervades the whole of nature but also penetrates within you.

The air you breathe is as natural as your breathing process. Pay attention to your breath, and realize that you are not doing it. It is the natural breath. If you had to remember to breathe, you would soon die; if you try to stop breathing, nature will overcome you. Through being aware of your breath, learning to keep your attention on the breath, you reconnect with nature in the most intimate and powerful way. Doing so is deeply healing and gives you great strength. It brings a shift of consciousness, from the conceptual world of thought, into the inner realm of infinite consciousness.
